implementation_notes: Rust closures capture by reference, by mutable reference or by value, as the compiler infers from how the body uses the captured variables, so the specialised function is simply `let add5 = |y| add(5, y);`, and when it must be returned or stored, `impl Fn(i32) -> i32` names the binding without boxing - Box<dyn Fn> is the type-erased alternative at API boundaries. move is the switch that matters: it forces the closure to own the bound value, which is what makes a returned specialisation sound, whereas a closure that borrows a local cannot escape it. Because closures are values with compile-time types, the classic binder structure has no counterpart; the remaining decision is FnOnce/FnMut/Fn and impl Trait versus dyn.
pitfalls: A closure that borrows a local cannot be returned (E0373 asks for move); with move the closure takes ownership of the captured value, which changes who may use that value afterwards.

FnOnce versus FnMut versus Fn: a closure that consumes a captured value (moving a String into the call, for example) can only be called once, so it cannot satisfy the Fn bound that iterator adaptors and callbacks require.
Box<dyn Fn> erases the concrete type, allocates and blocks inlining; keep it at API boundaries and prefer impl Fn for values that stay in one module.
